books.title: Clean Code
books.author: Robert C. Martin
books.usefulWhen: Doing everyday coding and code review: naming, small functions, tests.

books.title: A Philosophy of Software Design
books.author: John Ousterhout
books.usefulWhen: Designing APIs or modules, or refactoring shallow abstractions.

books.title: Clean Architecture
books.author: Robert C. Martin
books.usefulWhen: You need code that resists framework, database, and UI churn.

books.title: Code Complete
books.author: Steve McConnell
books.usefulWhen: You need disciplined implementation decisions on routines, control flow, and testing.

books.title: Designing Data-Intensive Applications
books.author: Martin Kleppmann
books.usefulWhen: Data ownership, event flows, or consistency semantics matter.

books.title: Domain-Driven Design
books.author: Eric Evans
books.usefulWhen: You want to model the business domain rather than tables, controllers, or DTOs.

books.title: Domain-Driven Design Distilled
books.author: Vaughn Vernon
books.usefulWhen: You want DDD benefits without heavy ceremony.

books.title: Implementing Domain-Driven Design
books.author: Vaughn Vernon
books.usefulWhen: You need implementation-level DDD: aggregates, events, and integrations.

books.title: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture
books.author: Martin Fowler
books.usefulWhen: You need to choose an appropriate enterprise pattern instead of mixing responsibilities.

books.title: Refactoring
books.author: Martin Fowler
books.usefulWhen: You want small, test-backed structural changes kept separate from feature work.

books.title: Refactoring.Guru
books.author: Refactoring.Guru (website)
books.usefulWhen: You need to diagnose smells, pick a safe treatment, and avoid uncontrolled redesign.

books.title: Release It!
books.author: Michael T. Nygard
books.usefulWhen: You are building services, APIs, queues, or critical production paths.

books.title: The Pragmatic Programmer
books.author: Andrew Hunt, David Thomas
books.usefulWhen: You want a general engineering layer: automation, feedback, orthogonality.

books.title: Working Effectively with Legacy Code
books.author: Michael Feathers
books.usefulWhen: You are changing poorly tested legacy code and need to regain control first.

entries.name: audit
entries.description: Scan a directory or repository for Clean Code health and return ranked hot spots in at most 40 lines.
entries.argumentHint: [directory | glob | empty for the repository root]

entries.name: boundaries
entries.description: Use when core logic calls a third-party library, SDK or service directly, when upgrading one, or when coding against an API that does not exist yet. Decides which vendor types and exceptions the core may see; wiring is clean-code-system-construction, failure design clean-code-error-handling.

entries.name: boy-scout
entries.description: Leave the code you touched cleaner than you found it: one worthwhile cleanup per touched area, inside the touched code, with tests. Reports what was left alone.
entries.argumentHint: [paths | empty for the files in the current diff]

entries.name: checklist
entries.description: Walk the Clean Code final checklist and hard rules against your current change, with a yes, no or not-applicable and a next action for each no.
entries.argumentHint: [paths | empty for the current diff]

entries.name: class-design
entries.description: Use when a class or module is growing, changes for several unrelated reasons, has fields used by only some methods, or is named Manager, Helper or Util. Judges one class's responsibilities; exposed surface is clean-code-data-and-objects, change spread across files is clean-code-smells-coupling.

entries.name: clean-tests
entries.description: Use when writing, reviewing or refactoring unit and integration tests, or when tests are slow, fragile, order-dependent or hard to read. Judges how a test is written; whether one is needed or written first is clean-code-tdd-discipline, flakiness from threads or timers is clean-code-concurrency.

entries.name: comments
entries.description: Use when adding, reviewing or deleting comments, TODO notes or commented-out code, or when a comment explains what code does. Decides which text may stay once names and structure are as clear as they can be; fix those first with clean-code-naming and clean-code-function-shape.

entries.name: concurrency
entries.description: Use when adding or changing threads, async tasks, locks, queues, workers, shutdown or cancellation, or when a test of such code fails intermittently. Decides whether concurrency is warranted and keeps shared state in check; a flaky test with no concurrency is clean-code-clean-tests.

entries.name: data-and-objects
entries.description: Use when designing or reviewing what a type exposes: getter and setter pairs, call chains through several objects, DTOs, or types that are half data and half behavior. Judges the public surface; class size and responsibilities are clean-code-class-design.

entries.name: emergent-design
entries.description: Use when choosing between two designs, deciding whether to add an abstraction, class, layer or dependency, or tempted to redesign. Applies the four-criteria tie-breaker and boring solutions; removing duplication, dead code or pass-through layers is clean-code-smells-redundancy.

entries.name: error-handling
entries.description: Use when writing or reviewing exceptions, error codes, null or absent returns, error messages, or cleanup and shutdown paths in your own code. Keeps the happy path readable and failures explicit and diagnosable; vendor exceptions caught at the edge are clean-code-boundaries.

entries.name: explain-rule
entries.description: Explain one Clean Code rule: its strength (must, should, must not), the reason, how to check it, an original example and the book's own exceptions.
entries.argumentHint: [rule name | section | situation you are unsure about]

entries.name: extract-till-you-drop
entries.description: Decompose one long function into single-level functions by extracting step by step with tests after each, and stop before the pieces become named fragments.
entries.argumentHint: [file:function | function name | empty for the longest function in the current diff]

entries.name: fix
entries.description: Resolve given Clean Code findings with the smallest change per finding, run the tests after each, and report. Never commits.
entries.argumentHint: [finding text | file:line | 'last review' | empty to ask]

entries.name: formatting
entries.description: Use when arranging a file, ordering functions, grouping related code, or reacting to formatting noise in a diff. Covers vertical ordering, proximity of related concepts, file size, line length, indentation, brittle alignment and formatter-first practice.

entries.name: function-contracts
entries.description: Use when a function takes many parameters, a boolean flag or an output argument, writes state while answering a question, or must be called in a hidden order. Judges signatures and declared effects, not the body (clean-code-function-shape) or behavior against the name (clean-code-smells-surprise).

entries.name: function-shape
entries.description: Use when a function is long, deeply nested, mixes levels of detail, or needs a comment to separate its phases. Judges the body: size, one abstraction level, nesting, negative conditionals. Signatures and effects are clean-code-function-contracts; which comments may stay is clean-code-comments.

entries.name: learning-tests
entries.description: Pin down how a third-party library already in the project behaves with small tests that call it the way you will, then propose the narrow local interface around it.
entries.argumentHint: [library or API | file where it is used | empty to find vendor usage in the diff]

entries.name: naming
entries.description: Use when naming or renaming variables, functions, types or constants, or when a reader cannot tell what an identifier means. Covers intention-revealing names, one word per concept, magic numbers and name smells. A comment that props up a weak name is fixed here first (clean-code-comments).

entries.name: plan
entries.description: Plan a non-trivial change with the Clean Code change process: intent, simplest correct change, tests first, validation and an explicit cleanup budget. Does not edit.
entries.argumentHint: [task description | issue text | empty to plan around the current diff]

entries.name: principles
entries.description: Applies the Clean Code rule set to everyday coding and review. Use for any task that writes, reviews or changes code where readability, names, function shape, side effects, comments, error handling, tests or cleanup of touched code matter.

entries.name: refactoring-steps
entries.description: Use when restructuring existing code without changing behavior, preparing for a change by cleaning first, or sequencing a cleanup. Covers small safe steps, make-it-work-then-right, rename, extract and inline moves, and stopping. Whether tests exist or come first is clean-code-tdd-discipline.

entries.name: review
entries.description: Review a diff or paths against the Clean Code rules and report ranked findings with file, line, rule, consequence and the smallest fix.
entries.argumentHint: [paths | git ref | empty for the current diff]

entries.name: smell-hunt
entries.description: Hunt the Clean Code smell catalog by family (names, functions, comments, design, tests) and map each hit to its treatment skill, in at most 40 lines.
entries.argumentHint: [names|functions|comments|design|tests|all] [paths | empty for the current diff]

entries.name: smells-coupling
entries.description: Use when one requirement edits many files, a base class mentions its subclasses, unrelated concepts share a type or constant, or the same type switch repeats. Judges dependencies between classes and files; one class's size or cohesion is clean-code-class-design.

entries.name: smells-redundancy
entries.description: Use when code repeats itself, contains unused code, or has layers that only forward calls. Smell family for duplicated logic, dead code, unused abstractions and indirection, with detection recipes. Removes proven waste; choosing between designs is clean-code-emergent-design.

entries.name: smells-surprise
entries.description: Use when code does not do the obvious thing its name promises, edge inputs behave wrongly, checks are disabled or suppressed, or behavior depends on hidden defaults. Judges observed behavior against the name; signature design and declared side effects are clean-code-function-contracts.

entries.name: successive-refinement
entries.description: Take a working but rough draft and refine it in named rounds (names, shape, duplication, contracts, tests) with the tests green after each, until the four design criteria hold.
entries.argumentHint: [feature description | file path | empty to refine the draft in the current diff]

entries.name: system-construction
entries.description: Use when business code creates its own collaborators, reads global configuration, wires dependencies mid-flow, or is cluttered by logging, transactions or retries. Decides where objects are built and wired; which vendor types the core may see is clean-code-boundaries.

entries.name: tdd-discipline
entries.description: Use when changing behavior, fixing a bug, or deciding how much to test. Covers failing-test-first, bug-fix tests, coverage as a signal, ignored tests and boundary cases. Decides whether and when tests exist; test quality is clean-code-clean-tests, restructuring is clean-code-refactoring-steps.

entries.name: vocabulary-audit
entries.description: Build the concept-to-term table for a directory: synonyms used for one concept and words used for two, with a recommended single term for each.
entries.argumentHint: [directory | glob | empty for the repository root]

entries.name: mode-campsite
entries.description: Does the requested task, then closes every answer that changed code with a Campsite block: what was left cleaner inside the touched code and what was deliberately not touched. A report format only; to run a cleanup on demand use clean-code-boy-scout.

entries.name: mode-mentor
entries.description: Teaches the Clean Code rule behind each decision, names it, and ends non-trivial answers with one short check-for-understanding question.

entries.name: mode-pair
entries.description: Works in small narrated steps with tests between them and asks before any change larger than a few lines or one that touches public API.

entries.name: mode-smell-first
entries.description: Names the smells in the code it is about to touch before any edit, ties each edit to a named smell and its treatment, and lists what remains afterwards.

entries.name: mode-strict-reviewer
entries.description: Answers as a ranked findings table against the Clean Code rules, never rewrites code unless asked, and says No findings explicitly when clean.

entries.name: mode-terse
entries.description: Result first, no preamble, a few lines at most unless asked, while still reporting what ran, the unresolved risk, and failing output in full.

entries.name: adapter-builder
entries.description: Implementer that wraps a third-party dependency behind a narrow interface in the core's vocabulary, reuses existing learning tests and adds only missing ones, and migrates callers one at a time. Use when boundary findings or clean-code-learning-tests output call for an adapter around an SDK or client.

entries.name: boundary-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of third-party and external dependency use: vendor types in core code, wide interfaces, untranslated errors and unpinned behavior. Use proactively after edits that import an SDK, ORM or HTTP client, or call an external service.

entries.name: class-design-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of class and module responsibility, cohesion and change locality, including coupling smells. Use proactively after edits that grow a class, add a module, add a subclass, or make one change touch many files.

entries.name: comment-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of comments and TODO notes. Use proactively after edits that add or change comments, leave commented-out code, add TODOs, or alter code that has comments attached.

entries.name: concurrency-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of concurrency and async code: whether it is needed, shared mutable state, lock scope, task lifecycle, cancellation, and testability under varied schedules. Use proactively after edits adding threads, async tasks, locks or background workers.

entries.name: construction-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of object construction and wiring: collaborators created inside business code, hidden lazy init, global lookups, bootstrapping that decides behavior, cross-cutting clutter. Use proactively after edits adding services, factories or startup code.

entries.name: contract-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of function signatures and effects: parameters, flags, output arguments, hidden side effects, command/query mixing and surprising behavior. Use proactively after edits that change signatures or add state changes.

entries.name: error-handling-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of failure design: exceptions, error codes, null and absent returns, error messages, swallowed errors and cleanup paths. Use proactively after edits that add try/catch, return null or error values, or acquire resources.

entries.name: final-gate
entries.description: Pre-merge gate that runs the Clean Code final checklist and hard rules against the working diff and returns PASS or FAIL with evidence. Use before declaring work done, committing or opening a pull request.

entries.name: function-extractor
entries.description: Implementer that decomposes one long function into single-level functions, extracting step by step with tests after each and stopping before the pieces become named fragments. Use when a function review finds an oversized or mixed-level function.

entries.name: function-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of function bodies: size, single purpose, abstraction levels, nesting and conditionals. Use proactively after edits that add or lengthen functions, add branches, or nest control flow.

entries.name: layout-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of file layout: vertical ordering, proximity of related code, file size, line length and brittle alignment. Use proactively after edits that add functions to a file, move code, or produce whitespace-heavy diffs.

entries.name: lead
entries.description: Triage lead for Clean Code work. Use first on any non-trivial change or review to decide which specialist reviewers, implementers and skills apply, in what order, and how much cleanup is proportionate. Routes only; does not review.

entries.name: naming-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of identifier names and vocabulary. Use proactively after edits that add or rename variables, functions, types or constants, or that introduce numeric or string literals with business meaning.

entries.name: object-design-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of what types expose: objects versus data carriers, getter and setter mirrors, call chains, smart DTOs and leaked representation. Use proactively after edits that add or change classes, records, DTOs or accessors.

entries.name: refactorer
entries.description: Implementer that carries out behavior-preserving structural changes in small, test-backed steps. Use when review findings or a plan call for renames, extractions, inlining, flag removal or dead-code deletion in a defined scope.

entries.name: scope-guard
entries.description: Reviewer that compares a diff with the request and classifies each hunk as required, enabling cleanup, opportunistic cleanup or out of scope. Use proactively after cleanup or refactoring, before final review, whenever a diff looks larger than the task.

entries.name: simplicity-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of unearned structure: speculative abstractions, pass-through layers, needless dependencies, duplicated rules, premature optimization. Use proactively after edits that add interfaces, factories, layers, dependencies or caching.

entries.name: smell-scanner
entries.description: Mechanical scanner that produces a census of smell candidates with numbers and locations: long functions, nesting, parameter counts, flags, commented-out code, skipped tests, suppressions. Use when you need raw counts before judgment.

entries.name: test-gap-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer that finds changed behavior with no protecting test: missing bug-fix tests, untested boundaries, skipped or ignored tests, multi-step builds. Use proactively after any behavior change or bug fix, before reporting work as done.

entries.name: test-quality-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of the quality of tests that exist: one idea per test, readable setup, determinism, isolation, speed and brittleness. Use proactively after edits that add or change tests, or when tests become slow or flaky.

entries.name: test-writer
entries.description: Implementer that writes clean tests first for behavior changes and bug fixes, shows each failing for the right reason, and edits test files only. Use when test-gap findings call for tests or before implementing specified behavior.

entries.name: audit
entries.description: Scan a directory or repository for complexity health and return clusters rated healthy, watch or hot plus ranked hot spots in at most 40 lines.
entries.argumentHint: [directory | glob | empty for the repository root]

entries.name: checklist
entries.description: Walk the book's final checklist against the current work with yes, no or not-applicable per item and a concrete next action for every no.
entries.argumentHint: [paths | git ref | empty for the current diff]

entries.name: collapse-layer
entries.description: Remove a forwarding layer or merge shallow fragments safely: move any real logic to the owner, repoint callers in small steps with tests, then delete the layer. Never commits.
entries.argumentHint: [class, file or module to collapse | empty to ask]

entries.name: comments-as-design
entries.description: Use when writing, reviewing or deleting comments and doc comments: contracts, invariants, hidden design decisions and rationale belong in comments; narration or excuses for poor names and structure do not.

entries.name: comments-first
entries.description: Draft the interface contract and explanatory comments for a module before writing its body, and revise the abstraction when the comment gets complicated. Outputs stubs, not implementations.
entries.argumentHint: [module, class or function to design | paths | empty to draft contracts for new public elements in the diff]

entries.name: complexity-symptoms
entries.description: Use when a change feels awkward, one edit touches many files, a reader must reconstruct hidden dependencies, or you must judge whether a design got simpler. Names the symptom and asks the default-response questions before any edit.

entries.name: deep-modules
entries.description: Use when designing or reviewing a class, module, service or package: judge whether its interface is small and meaningful relative to the work it hides, and whether it carries its own weight.

entries.name: define-errors-away
entries.description: Use when adding validation, try/catch, null checks or error codes, or when many callers repeat the same defensive handling. Redesigns the interface or invariant so the exception case does not exist, instead of adding more checks.

entries.name: depth-map
entries.description: Inventory the modules in a scope by interface weight and hidden work, and return the shallow and pass-through ones ranked, in at most 40 lines.
entries.argumentHint: [directory | glob | empty for the repository root]

entries.name: design-alternatives
entries.description: Use before committing to a non-trivial interface, abstraction or decomposition, and whenever two or more designs are being weighed: compare at least two plausible designs on interface simplicity, information hiding, special-case reduction and future cognitive load.

entries.name: design-twice
entries.description: Write two or more designs for an interface or module as call sites, score them on the rule set's four criteria, choose one and record the price. Does not edit.
entries.argumentHint: [problem statement | paths | empty to compare the design in the current diff]

entries.name: explain-rule
entries.description: Explain one rule of A Philosophy of Software Design: its modal strength, the reason, how to check it, an original example and where the book allows an exception.
entries.argumentHint: [rule name | topic | upstream section | empty to list topics]

entries.name: fix
entries.description: Resolve given design findings with the smallest change per finding, run the tests after each, and report. Never commits.
entries.argumentHint: [finding text | file:line | 'last review' | empty to ask]

entries.name: flags-and-knobs
entries.description: Use when the signature itself has a boolean or mode parameter that switches behavior, an options bag that keeps growing, or a callback added so one caller can override a step. Decides inside or splits by intent. Not for lines repeated at call sites.

entries.name: functions-and-variables
entries.description: Use when splitting a long function, extracting tiny helpers, or adding intermediate variables inside one function body: judge each by whether it hides meaningful work and captures meaning, not by line counts.

entries.name: generality-and-special-cases
entries.description: Use when an interface fits exactly one caller, an abstraction is so general it says nothing, or a few rare cases clutter the core path with conditionals. Sets the generality level and isolates special behavior.

entries.name: information-hiding
entries.description: Use when deciding where knowledge belongs: one decision or format (file format, storage shape, protocol detail, internal representation, normalization or edge handling) known by several modules, or workflow bookkeeping exposed to callers.

entries.name: interface-design
entries.description: Use when shaping a single public function, method, class or API element as a whole: design it around what callers need to know, not how the implementation works. Narrow but meaningful, names that reveal the abstraction. Behavior-switching parameters are flags-and-knobs.

entries.name: naming-and-obviousness
entries.description: Use when naming or renaming modules, methods, parameters and variables, when related operations differ in naming or argument order, or when code surprises a reader. Names reveal the abstraction; surprise counts as complexity.

entries.name: pass-through-layers
entries.description: Use when a class, service, facade, adapter or helper module mostly forwards calls, wraps a library without simplifying it, or only renames obvious operations; also before adding such a layer.

entries.name: performance-and-trends
entries.description: Use when asked to optimize, when a cache or micro-optimization is proposed, or when a pattern, paradigm, framework or fashionable technique is about to be adopted. Requires evidence and hides optimizations behind stable interfaces.

entries.name: plan
entries.description: Plan a non-trivial change with the book's generation sequence: concept, narrowest interface, hidden details, caller impact, special cases, alternatives and scope. Does not edit.
entries.argumentHint: [task description | issue text | paths | empty to plan from the current diff]

entries.name: principles
entries.description: Applies A Philosophy of Software Design to module, API and refactoring decisions. Use for any task that creates, reviews or changes code where complexity, module depth, information hiding, interface shape or tactical patching matter.

entries.name: pull-complexity-down
entries.description: Use when the same preparation, normalization or default-choosing lines are repeated at the call sites of one callee, or every caller must remember a rule to call it correctly. The fix is more work inside the callee. Repeated error handling is define-errors-away.

entries.name: review
entries.description: Review a diff or paths against A Philosophy of Software Design and report findings ranked by complexity cost.
entries.argumentHint: [paths | git ref | empty for the current diff]

entries.name: split-or-merge
entries.description: Use when deciding whether to extract, split or merge units larger than a function (classes, files, services, packages), or when understanding one idea means jumping through shallow fragments or a module hides two unrelated decisions.

entries.name: strategic-programming
entries.description: Use when the change is a deadline patch or a copy-paste of existing code, the same workaround is about to appear a third time, or recurring friction suggests reshaping an abstraction. Sizes the design investment; it does not choose a signature shape.

entries.name: symptom-trace
entries.description: Trace a complaint such as 'this change touched too many files' or 'I cannot follow this' from the symptom to its likely cause with history evidence, and name the skill that treats it.
entries.argumentHint: [complaint text | paths | git ref | empty to look for co-changing files in recent history]

entries.name: temporal-decomposition
entries.description: Use when code is organized as prepare/process/finalize phases, objects need staged calls before use, init/open/configure sequences exist, or callers must know a hidden call order.

entries.name: testing-through-interfaces
entries.description: Use when writing or reviewing tests for modules with hidden complexity: test public behavior and contracts, add focused tests for isolated special cases, and avoid tests that need implementation details or force leaky interfaces.

entries.name: mode-architect
entries.description: Designs before coding: states the abstraction, the narrowest interface, what it hides and what callers no longer need to know, and compares two designs for non-trivial choices.

entries.name: mode-complexity-ledger
entries.description: Ends every code answer with a short complexity ledger: facts a reader must hold, files a similar future change touches, special cases at call sites, public surface and net direction, before and after.

entries.name: mode-mentor
entries.description: Teaches the design principle behind each decision, names it, shows what it costs a reader, and checks understanding with one short question.

entries.name: mode-pair
entries.description: Works in small narrated steps, says what complexity each step removes, and asks before any change larger than a few lines, a new module or layer, or anything touching public API.

entries.name: mode-strict-reviewer
entries.description: Answers as a ranked findings table with the complexity cost of each finding, rewrites no code unless asked, and says No findings explicitly.

entries.name: mode-terse
entries.description: Result first, no preamble, a few lines unless asked, with failing output still in full. Brevity applies to prose, never to the clarity of the design.

entries.name: caller-burden-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of work pushed onto callers: repeated setup, conversions, guards and workarounds around one function that its owner could absorb. Use proactively after edits that add a parameter, a required step, or the same lines before several calls.

entries.name: comment-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of comments as design: gives every comment in the change a disposition and lists public elements that lack a contract. Use proactively after edits that add or alter doc comments, inline comments, or public elements.

entries.name: complexity-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of the net complexity change in a diff, judged by symptom: change amplification, cognitive load, unknown unknowns, hidden dependencies, spread and temporal coupling. Use proactively after a change that felt awkward or touched many files.

entries.name: contract-writer
entries.description: Implementer that edits comments only: writes interface contracts, invariants and decision notes, deletes narration, and reports where a contract cannot be written briefly. Use when public elements lack contracts or comments mislead.

entries.name: depth-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of module depth: interface weight against hidden work, and pass-through layers, thin wrappers and rename-only helpers. Use proactively after edits that add classes, services, wrappers, facades or helper modules.

entries.name: evidence-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of added complexity that claims a benefit: optimizations, caches, patterns, frameworks and paradigms. Checks for evidence, and for the complexity staying behind a stable interface. Use proactively after performance changes or when a new pattern or framework appears.

entries.name: exception-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of error surface: exceptions, error codes, null checks and validation that could be defined away, handled inside the module, or must stay. Use proactively after edits that add throws, try/catch, guards or error types.

entries.name: final-gate
entries.description: Pre-merge gate that runs the book's review checklist against the working diff and returns PASS or FAIL with evidence per item. Use before declaring work done, committing, or opening a pull request.

entries.name: function-depth-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of function bodies and variables: fragment chains, pass-through variables, syntax-mirroring names, leaked intermediate state and long functions that really mix concepts. Use proactively after edits that extract helpers or introduce variables inside a function, and after large new functions.

entries.name: interface-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of public interface shape: boolean and mode parameters, option bags, mechanism-revealing arguments and caller-oriented signatures. Use proactively after edits that add or change a public function, method, class or endpoint.

entries.name: interface-simplifier
entries.description: Implementer that replaces boolean and mode parameters, option bags and mechanism-revealing arguments with caller-oriented operations and updates the callers. Collapses a setup sequence only when a finding names it. Use when findings call for simpler signatures in a defined scope.

entries.name: lead
entries.description: Triage lead for A Philosophy of Software Design work. Use first on any non-trivial change or review to decide which specialist reviewers, implementers and skills apply, in what order, and how much restructuring is proportionate. Routes only; does not review.

entries.name: leakage-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of information hiding: which modules know a format, storage shape, protocol, representation or piece of bookkeeping. Use proactively after edits that add public members, change data shapes, or touch both sides of a file, wire or storage format.

entries.name: module-deepener
entries.description: Implementer that collapses forwarding layers, merges shallow fragments and moves work repeated by callers into the owning module, in small test-backed steps. Use when review findings or a depth map call for deeper modules in a defined scope.

entries.name: naming-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of names and obviousness: mechanism-revealing or vague names, inconsistent sibling operations, and behavior that would surprise a reader. Use proactively after edits that add public names, rename things, or add a variant of an existing operation.

entries.name: special-case-isolator
entries.description: Implementer that moves rare-case branches out of a core path into named, isolated places while keeping behavior identical, after pinning each moved case's current behavior. Use when review findings show special cases cluttering a general function.

entries.name: special-case-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of generality and special cases: interfaces fitted to one caller, abstractions too vague to say anything, and rare branches cluttering core paths. Use proactively after edits that add conditionals keyed on customers, regions, flags or legacy data.

entries.name: split-merge-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of boundaries between units: extractions, new files, classes and services, and boundaries kept by habit. Decides keep, merge or split by total complexity. Use proactively after edits that add, move, merge or split classes, files, services or packages.

entries.name: tactical-patch-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of how a change was made: quick symptom patches, copy-paste, extra flags, newly exposed details and added exception paths versus structural fixes. Use proactively after bug fixes and deadline work.

entries.name: temporal-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of time-shaped design: prepare/process/finalize modules, init-before-use objects, required call orders and partial objects, and where each ordering rule is enforced. Use proactively after edits that add setup, init, open or configure steps.

entries.name: test-contract-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of how tests couple to the design: assertions on private state or call order, members exposed only for tests, missing tests for isolated special cases. Use proactively after tests are added or after a refactor breaks many tests.

entries.name: test-writer
entries.description: Implementer that writes tests from a stated contract, one per guarantee and edge behavior, through the public interface only. Use when a module's promises are unpinned, before or after a structural change by someone else. Writes test files only; never edits or restructures production code.

entries.name: audit
entries.description: Scan a directory or repository for Clean Architecture health, rate each rule cluster, and return ranked hot spots in at most 40 lines.
entries.argumentHint: [directory | glob | empty for the repository root]

entries.name: boundary-economics
entries.description: Use when deciding whether, where and how heavy a boundary should be, when a shortcut is proposed under deadline pressure, or when a compromise is unavoidable. Shaping a justified port is ports-and-gateways; code already crossing a process or device edge is service-and-device-edges.

entries.name: boundary-models
entries.description: Use when a use case, entity or core service signature takes or returns a web request, ORM row, framework context or response object, or when request and response models are designed. Controller and mapper bodies are interface-adapters; the action itself is use-cases.

entries.name: checklist
entries.description: Walk the Clean Architecture review checklist against your current change, with yes, no, unproven or n/a for each item and a next action for each open one.
entries.argumentHint: [paths | empty for the current diff]

entries.name: component-coupling
entries.description: Use when two packages or modules depend on each other, a stable component depends on a volatile one, or an abstract component has no reason to exist. Covers cycles, stability and abstractness. Layer import direction is dependency-rule, component membership is component-grouping.

entries.name: component-grouping
entries.description: Use when deciding which classes ship, version or change together, or how to split a codebase into packages, modules or deployables. Covers cohesion and release pressure. Cycles and stability belong to component-coupling, folder names and layout to screaming-structure.

entries.name: composition-root
entries.description: Use when deciding where objects are built and wired, when a use case or entity instantiates infrastructure, or when a constructor gains a dependency. Covers the main component and explicit construction. Interface design belongs to ports-and-gateways, container annotations to framework-independence.

entries.name: dependency-rule
entries.description: Use when judging or writing an import between your own layers, a package dependency or an interface's home layer, or when inner code reaches outward. Covers import direction. Framework markers go to framework-independence, ORM and SQL to persistence-independence, cycles to component-coupling.

entries.name: enforce-boundaries
entries.description: Make the layer rules fail a test or a build: choose the mechanism with the user from tooling the project already has, add the check, freeze known violations as a baseline, and prove the check can fail. Runs the tests, never commits.
entries.argumentHint: [tool name | layer description | empty to detect the tooling]

entries.name: entities-and-invariants
entries.description: Use when a business rule needs a home, an entity can reach an invalid state, or domain code does I/O or reads configuration. A rule already sitting in a controller or job: the destination is here, judging the controller itself is interface-adapters. One action's flow is use-cases.

entries.name: explain-rule
entries.description: Explain one Clean Architecture rule: its strength (MUST, SHOULD, MUST NOT), the reason, how to check it, an original example and the rule set's own exceptions.
entries.argumentHint: [rule name | section | situation you are unsure about]

entries.name: extract-use-case
entries.description: Move the rules and orchestration out of one handler, controller, job or service method into a use case with request and response models and ports, keeping behavior. Runs the tests, never commits.
entries.argumentHint: [file:line | function or method name | empty to ask]

entries.name: fix
entries.description: Resolve given Clean Architecture findings with the smallest change per finding, run the tests after each, and report. Never commits.
entries.argumentHint: [finding text | file:line | 'last review' | empty to ask]

entries.name: framework-independence
entries.description: Use when framework annotations, decorators, base classes, middleware, serializers or context objects appear in domain or use case code. Covers keeping the framework at the edge. Database and ORM markers belong to persistence-independence, imports between your own layers to dependency-rule.

entries.name: interface-adapters
entries.description: Use when writing or judging controllers, presenters, mappers or gateway implementations, including one that skips a use case or branches on business fields. Rule destination: entities-and-invariants or use-cases. Signature types: boundary-models; consumers, devices: service-and-device-edges.

entries.name: introduce-port
entries.description: Replace one direct use of a volatile dependency in core code with a policy-owned port, an adapter and wiring in the composition root, plus a fake for tests. Runs the tests, never commits.
entries.argumentHint: [file:line of the direct use | dependency name | empty to ask]

entries.name: inward-refactoring
entries.description: Use only when asked to restructure existing code toward Clean Architecture in safe steps: wrapping details, replacing concrete dependencies with ports, splitting god services, ordering several findings. Where a moved rule lands is entities-and-invariants; the target shape is in its cluster skill.

entries.name: layer-map
entries.description: Discover the layers a repository really has and the direction of the imports between them. Returns a ranked layer table, an import matrix and the outward edges, in at most 40 lines.
entries.argumentHint: [directory | empty for the repository root]

entries.name: new-feature
entries.description: Build a new feature in the order Clean Architecture gives: domain rule, use case, boundary interfaces, presenter and gateway contracts, adapters, wiring. Skips layers the feature does not need. Runs the tests, never commits.
entries.argumentHint: [feature description | ticket text | empty to ask]

entries.name: persistence-independence
entries.description: Use when the domain model is shaped by tables, when SQL, ORM mappings or gateway code carry business rules, or when rules need a real database. Web and injection markers belong to framework-independence, import direction to dependency-rule, port ownership and naming to ports-and-gateways.

entries.name: place-code
entries.description: Classify a function, class or snippet statement by statement as business policy, orchestration, translation or infrastructure, and say which layer each part belongs in. Read-only; it reports where code belongs and edits nothing.
entries.argumentHint: [file:line | function or class name | pasted snippet | empty for the current diff]

entries.name: plan
entries.description: Plan a non-trivial change with Clean Architecture: the use case, its models and ports, where each piece lives, the boundary decisions and the build order, without editing anything.
entries.argumentHint: [feature or change description | ticket text | empty to ask]

entries.name: ports-and-gateways
entries.description: Use when core code builds or calls a database, mailer, payment provider, clock or ID generator directly, or when choosing which layer owns and names an interface. Construction sites are composition-root, storage leaks are persistence-independence, whether a port pays off is boundary-economics.

entries.name: principles
entries.description: Applies the Clean Architecture rule set to design and code decisions. Use for any task that creates, reviews or changes code where dependency direction, business policy independence, boundaries, use cases or replaceable frameworks and databases matter.

entries.name: review
entries.description: Review a diff or paths against the Clean Architecture rules and report ranked findings with concrete refactoring proposals.
entries.argumentHint: [paths | git ref | empty for the current diff]

entries.name: screaming-structure
entries.description: Use when creating or reorganizing folders, packages, modules or class names, or when the tree shows only controllers, services and models. Covers feature and use-case first layout, role-based naming and the default feature shape. What ships or changes together is component-grouping.

entries.name: service-and-device-edges
entries.description: Use when code crosses a process or network boundary, consumes messages, wraps a remote service, or talks to hardware. Covers humble listeners, remote calls as I/O and device interfaces. In-process controllers belong to interface-adapters; whether to split a service is boundary-economics.

entries.name: service-sprawl
entries.description: Use when a *Service, *Manager or *Helper class keeps growing, owns unrelated use cases, or creates, fetches, validates, persists, publishes and presents in one place. Covers splitting god services by use case. Shared modules are shared-code-coupling; interface and subtype design is solid-design.

entries.name: shared-code-coupling
entries.description: Use when about to remove duplication, create or grow a common, shared, utils, base or core module, or merge use cases for convenience. Covers when sharing couples different actors and when duplication is the right choice. A single growing class is service-sprawl.

entries.name: solid-design
entries.description: Use when judging class and interface design: fat interfaces, substitutable implementations, extension without editing stable policy, or inverting a dependency with polymorphism. A catch-all Service class is service-sprawl, interface ownership is ports-and-gateways.

entries.name: testing-seams
entries.description: Use when writing, placing or judging tests for entities, use cases, adapters or boundary contracts, or when business rules can only be tested with a framework, database or network. Covers core-first tests, fakes and adapter tests. What a use case contains is use-cases.

entries.name: use-cases
entries.description: Use when writing or reshaping one application action: a use case class or function, its orchestration and the order to build a feature. Types crossing its boundary are boundary-models, rules that hold for every action are entities-and-invariants, tests are testing-seams.

entries.name: mode-architect
entries.description: States the use case and a placement table before writing code, lists the arrows of every new dependency, and ends each change with a dependency direction check.

entries.name: mode-boundary-budget
entries.description: Justifies every proposed port, layer, package or service with a one-line cost versus option value entry and the lighter alternative, and tallies built, skipped and compromised boundaries.

entries.name: mode-mentor
entries.description: Teaches the Clean Architecture rule behind each decision, with its strength, and checks understanding with one question.

entries.name: mode-pair
entries.description: Works in small narrated steps, states intent before each move, and asks before any change larger than a few lines or touching a public name or an interface.

entries.name: mode-strict-reviewer
entries.description: Answers review requests as a ranked findings table with rule, evidence and minimal fix; never rewrites code unless asked; says No findings explicitly.

entries.name: mode-terse
entries.description: Result first, no preamble, a few lines at most unless asked, with a one-line dependency direction verdict; failing output is still shown in full.

entries.name: adapter-humility-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of adapters: controllers, presenters, mappers and gateway implementations that hold business decisions or skip the use case. Use proactively after edits to routes, handlers, jobs, presenters, repositories or gateway classes.

entries.name: architecture-test-writer
entries.description: Test author that writes the executable layer-rule check with the tooling the project already has, with a baseline for known violations. Use when the dependency rule exists only in a diagram or in habit. Edits test and build configuration only.

entries.name: boundary-cost-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of boundary decisions: boundaries that are missing, overbuilt or unenforced, and compromises without a note. Use proactively after edits that add a port, layer, package, queue or service, or when a shortcut skips a boundary.

entries.name: boundary-model-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of the types that cross the core boundary: requests, rows, framework objects and response types in use case and entity signatures. Use proactively after edits that change a use case signature, a mapper, a DTO or a model class.

entries.name: component-coupling-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of dependencies between components: cycles, stable components depending on volatile ones, and abstract components without a reason to exist. Use proactively after edits that add imports between packages or modules, or change a package split.

entries.name: domain-purity-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of the domain layer: whether entities guard their invariants and whether domain code is free of I/O, configuration reads and clock calls. Use proactively after edits to entities, domain services or any code that holds a business rule.

entries.name: feature-builder
entries.description: Implementer that builds a new feature inside out: domain rule, use case, boundary interfaces, adapters and wiring, skipping layers the feature does not need. Use when a requirement for new behavior is ready to be built.

entries.name: final-gate
entries.description: Pre-merge gate that runs the Clean Architecture review checklist against the working diff and returns PASS or FAIL with evidence per item. Use before declaring work done, committing or opening a pull request.

entries.name: import-direction-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of import direction between layers, including framework, ORM, driver and vendor imports in domain or application code. Use proactively after edits that add imports, declare interfaces or touch domain and use case files.

entries.name: import-scanner
entries.description: Mechanical scanner that counts imports per directory and lists outward-looking candidates without judging them. Use when a reviewer or the lead needs a raw import census of a tree before layers or components are judged.

entries.name: interface-contract-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of interface and subtype design: fat interfaces, unsubstitutable implementations, policy edited per variant, needless extension points. Use proactively after edits that add an interface, an implementation, a subclass or a type switch.

entries.name: lead
entries.description: Triage lead for Clean Architecture work. Use first on any non-trivial change or review to decide which specialist reviewers, implementers and skills apply, in what order, and how much structure is proportionate. Routes only; does not review.

entries.name: port-introducer
entries.description: Implementer that replaces named direct uses of volatile dependencies in core code with policy-owned ports, adapters, fakes and composition-root wiring. Use when review findings call for isolating a database, client, clock, mailer or file system.

entries.name: port-ownership-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of ports and gateways: whether volatile dependencies sit behind interfaces owned by the inner layer and named by role. Use proactively after edits that call a client, SDK, clock, ID generator or file system, or that declare an interface.

entries.name: seam-test-writer
entries.description: Test author that writes core tests for entities and use cases with fakes for ports, plus separate adapter tests. Use when policy has no tests that run without a framework, database or network. Edits test files only.

entries.name: service-edge-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of process, network and device edges: message listeners, webhooks, remote clients and hardware access. Use proactively after edits to consumers, scheduled triggers, service clients, firmware or driver code.

entries.name: sprawl-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of code accumulation: god services, Manager and Helper classes, and shared, common or utils modules that couple different actors. Use proactively after edits that grow a Service class, add to a shared module, or extract duplicated code.

entries.name: structure-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of folder layout and names: whether the tree announces use cases or frameworks, and whether grouping follows cohesion and release pressure. Use proactively after edits that add or move packages, folders or classes, or rename modules.

entries.name: test-seam-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of where tests sit relative to the architectural seams: rule tests that need a framework, database or network, and adapters without tests of their own. Use proactively after edits that add or change tests, or change a use case or adapter.

entries.name: use-case-extractor
entries.description: Implementer that moves the rules and orchestration of existing handlers, controllers, jobs or service methods into use cases with request and response models and ports, test-backed. Use when review findings call for extracting several actions.

entries.name: use-case-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of use cases: one application action, explicit input and output, ports for external effects, orchestration only. Use proactively after edits that add or change a use case, an application service or a handler that coordinates a workflow.

entries.name: wiring-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of object construction and wiring: infrastructure built inside policy code, configuration reads in business code, service locators. Use proactively after edits that add a constructor argument, a new client, a container registration or a main component.

entries.name: assertions-and-contracts
entries.description: Use when a routine relies on assumptions about inputs, state or results: write preconditions, postconditions, invariants; choose assertion, validation or domain error. External input: code-complete-trust-boundaries. Expected failures: code-complete-error-handling.

entries.name: audit
entries.description: Scan a directory or repository for Code Complete construction health and return cluster ratings and ranked hot spots in at most 40 lines.
entries.argumentHint: [directory | glob | empty for the repository root]

entries.name: checklist
entries.description: Walk the Code Complete review checklist against your current change with yes, no or n/a per question and a next action for each no.
entries.argumentHint: [paths | empty for the current diff]

entries.name: class-design
entries.description: Use when a class or module has several responsibilities, exposes internals, mixes persistence, formatting, business rules and integration, or reaches into another's internals. Covers cohesion and coupling. One routine: code-complete-routine-design.

entries.name: coding-standards
entries.description: Use when naming, formatting, file structure or idioms diverge from the codebase, or when reformatting and renaming noise appears in a diff that is not about style. Comment content belongs to code-complete-comments.

entries.name: comments
entries.description: Use when adding, reviewing or deleting comments, or when a comment restates code, is stale, or props up unclear code. Comments keep intent, rationale, contracts. Style and layout: code-complete-coding-standards.

entries.name: complexity-management
entries.description: Use when code is hard to hold in your head: tangled routines, duplicated logic, clever expressions, growing special cases. One branch: code-complete-control-flow. One routine: code-complete-routine-design. To refactor: code-complete-refactoring-judgment.

entries.name: construction-process
entries.description: Use before a non-trivial change: work starting from a proposed solution, unsettled decisions, or slicing into verifiable increments with early integration. Written plan: code-complete-plan. One routine: code-complete-routine-design.

entries.name: control-flow
entries.description: Use when branches are hard to verify: deep nesting, compound conditions, switch statements, multiple exits, dead branches, side-effecting conditions. Loops and statement order: code-complete-statements-and-loops. Repeated mappings: code-complete-table-driven.

entries.name: data-types
entries.description: Use when a value's meaning must be decoded: magic numbers, sentinels like -1, units, boolean flags, status strings, parallel arrays. Choose types and constants. Variable lifetime: code-complete-variables. Flag parameters in a signature: code-complete-routine-interface.

entries.name: debugging
entries.description: Use when something fails, throws, hangs or returns wrong results and the cause is unknown: reproduce, isolate, explain, fix, verify, add the regression test. No known failure: code-complete-routine-testing. Designing the failure path: code-complete-error-handling.

entries.name: error-handling
entries.description: Use when writing or reviewing the failure path: exceptions, error codes, catch blocks, messages, fallbacks. Unknown cause: code-complete-debugging. Valid input: code-complete-trust-boundaries. Programmer errors: code-complete-assertions-and-contracts.

entries.name: explain-rule
entries.description: Explain one Code Complete rule: its strength (binding, strong default or forbidden), the reason, how to check it, an original example and the source's own exceptions.
entries.argumentHint: [rule name | upstream section | situation you are unsure about]

entries.name: fix
entries.description: Resolve given Code Complete findings with the smallest change per finding, run the tests after each, and report. Never commits.
entries.argumentHint: [finding text | file:line | 'last review' | empty to ask]

entries.name: performance-tuning
entries.description: Use when asked to optimize or speed up, or when a change trades clarity for speed. Needs a requirement and before/after numbers. No speed goal: code-complete-refactoring-judgment or code-complete-complexity-management.

entries.name: plan
entries.description: Plan a non-trivial change before editing: restate the requirement, settle the construction decisions, list risks, cut verifiable increments and choose the test cases. Does not edit.
entries.argumentHint: [task description | issue text | empty to plan around the current diff]

entries.name: principles
entries.description: Applies the Code Complete rules to everyday construction work: any task that writes, changes, reviews, debugs or tunes code where defect risk, readability, data meaning, control flow or tests matter. A matching topical skill wins; sequencing a large change: code-complete-construction-process.

entries.name: pseudocode
entries.description: Design one complex routine with the Pseudocode Programming Process: sketch the steps, refine them to one abstraction level, convert to code, then prune the comments that only restate code.
entries.argumentHint: [routine description | file:routine | empty to ask]

entries.name: refactoring-judgment
entries.description: Use when deciding whether and how to refactor: structure hides intent, duplicates knowledge or raises defect risk, or refactoring mixes with behavior change or no tests. Symptoms: code-complete-complexity-management. Speed motive: code-complete-performance-tuning.

entries.name: review
entries.description: Review a diff or paths against the Code Complete rules and report ranked findings with file, line, rule, consequence and the smallest fix.
entries.argumentHint: [paths | git ref | empty for the current diff]

entries.name: routine-design
entries.description: Use when writing or reviewing a routine's body and name: unclear purpose, a name that does not fit, validation, computation and side effects mixed, hidden effects. Signatures: code-complete-routine-interface. Tangles across routines: code-complete-complexity-management.

entries.name: routine-interface
entries.description: Use when a routine's signature is the problem: long parameter lists, boolean mode flags, unrelated parameters, or return values that are easy to misuse. Body and naming: code-complete-routine-design. Flag fields and sentinels in data: code-complete-data-types.

entries.name: routine-testing
entries.description: Use when writing or reviewing tests for a routine: normal, boundary and invalid inputs, defensive checks, contract alignment, table-driven cases. A failure of unknown cause: code-complete-debugging.

entries.name: statements-and-loops
entries.description: Use when writing or reviewing loops and straight-line code: loop start, stop and update, bloated loop bodies, statement order, negated conditions, normal-path placement. Branch shape: code-complete-control-flow.

entries.name: table-driven
entries.description: Use when repeated if/else or switch chains map stable categories, ranges, conversions or dispatch to results, or a lookup table needs validating. Other branch problems: code-complete-control-flow.

entries.name: test-matrix
entries.description: Derive the normal, boundary, invalid and defensive-check test cases for one routine from its contract, as a table, before any test is written. Does not edit.
entries.argumentHint: [file:routine | routine name | empty to use the routine in the current diff]

entries.name: trust-boundaries
entries.description: Use when code takes input from users, files, networks, other services or callers you do not control: decide what is validated, rejected, recovered, logged. Internal assumptions: code-complete-assertions-and-contracts. How a failure travels: code-complete-error-handling.

entries.name: trust-boundary-scan
entries.description: Inventory the places where external input enters a directory or repository, and rate how each one validates, rejects, recovers, asserts and stays diagnosable. At most 40 lines.
entries.argumentHint: [directory | glob | empty for the repository root]

entries.name: tune
entries.description: Run a measured tuning loop on one target: confirm the requirement, take a baseline, change one thing, remeasure, keep or revert, and record the clarity trade-off. Never commits.
entries.argumentHint: [routine or endpoint to speed up | requirement such as 'p95 under 200 ms' | empty to ask]

entries.name: variables
entries.description: Use when a variable is vaguely named, declared far from use, reused for a second meaning, uninitialized or mutable without need. Types, constants, units, sentinels: code-complete-data-types.

entries.name: mode-assumptions-first
entries.description: Lists the inputs, trust boundaries and assumptions before writing or changing code, then shows where each is validated, asserted or tested when the change is done.

entries.name: mode-evidence-first
entries.description: Claims no cause, fix, refactoring safety or speedup without an evidence line: a reproduction, a test result or a measurement; unproven claims are labelled and never stated as fact.

entries.name: mode-mentor
entries.description: Teaches the Code Complete rule behind each construction decision, names it, and ends non-trivial answers with one short check-for-understanding question.

entries.name: mode-pair
entries.description: Works in small narrated steps with a test run between them, and asks before any change larger than a few lines or one that touches public API.

entries.name: mode-strict-reviewer
entries.description: Answers as a ranked findings table against the Code Complete rules, never rewrites code unless asked, and says No findings explicitly when clean.

entries.name: mode-terse
entries.description: Result first, no preamble, a few lines at most unless asked, while still reporting what ran, the unresolved risk, and failing output in full.

entries.name: boundary-hardener
entries.description: Implementer that adds boundary validation and internal assertions where review found a defensive gap, converting raw input to a typed value at the entry and adding rejection tests. Use when trust-boundary or contract findings call for checks.

entries.name: bug-fixer
entries.description: Implementer that fixes one reproduced defect by diagnosis: reproduce, isolate, explain, fix the root cause with the smallest change, add the regression test, verify. Use when a failure has an unknown cause and a fix is wanted, not just an opinion.

entries.name: class-design-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of class and module design: single responsibility, cohesion, exposed representation, mixed persistence, formatting and business concerns, and coupling to internals. Use proactively after edits that grow a class, add a module or widen a public surface.

entries.name: comment-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of comments: each gets a disposition of keep, rewrite, delete or replace with code. Use proactively after edits that add or change comments, leave commented-out code, or alter code that has comments attached.

entries.name: complexity-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of rising complexity: tangled routines, duplicated rules, dense clever expressions and special-case growth. Use proactively after edits that add flags or special cases, copy a block, or compress logic into one expression.

entries.name: consistency-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of consistency with the surrounding codebase: naming, idioms, layout, file structure and unrelated reformatting. Use proactively after edits that add new files or modules, or when a diff contains renames and formatting changes.

entries.name: construction-scanner
entries.description: Mechanical scanner that produces a census of construction candidates with numbers and locations: routine lengths, parameter counts, nesting, boolean parameters, literals, empty handlers, commented-out code. Use when you want raw counts before a review or audit.

entries.name: contract-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of the assumptions between routines: preconditions, postconditions, invariants, and whether each check is an assertion, validation or domain error. Use proactively after edits to routines with unstated call orders or state rules.

entries.name: control-flow-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of branches, loops and statement order: nesting, compound conditions, exits, dead branches, loop termination and update, negated conditions. Use proactively after edits that add conditions, loops or switch cases.

entries.name: data-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of data meaning and variable lifetime: magic values, sentinels, units, boolean flags, closed sets, scope, initialization and variable reuse. Use proactively after edits that add literals, flags, status fields or new locals.

entries.name: error-flow-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of failure paths: handler level, preserved context, consistency across routines, swallowed errors and silent fallbacks. Use proactively after edits that add try/catch, catch blocks, error returns, messages or fallback values.

entries.name: final-gate
entries.description: Pre-merge gate that runs the Code Complete review checklist and the five forbidden patterns against the working diff and returns PASS or FAIL with evidence. Use before declaring work done, committing or opening a pull request.

entries.name: increment-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of the shape of a change as an increment: behavior mixed with refactoring, hunks that cannot be verified alone, stranded or orphaned partial work. Use proactively after a sizeable edit and before opening a pull request.

entries.name: interface-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of routine signatures: parameter lists, boolean mode flags, unrelated parameters and return values that are easy to misuse. Use proactively after edits that add or change a signature or add a parameter to an existing one.

entries.name: lead
entries.description: Triage lead for Code Complete work. Use first on any non-trivial change or review to decide which specialist reviewers, implementers and skills apply, and in what order. Routes only; does not review the code itself.

entries.name: refactorer
entries.description: Implementer that carries out behavior-preserving structural changes in small, test-backed steps against named findings. Use when review findings or a plan call for renames, extractions, guard clauses, named predicates, tables or class splits in a defined scope.

entries.name: routine-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of routine purpose, name, phase separation and hidden effects. Use proactively after edits that add or lengthen routines, mix validation with computation and writes, or rename a routine.

entries.name: table-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of repeated branching that is a table in disguise, and of existing lookup tables that are incomplete, overlapping or unvalidated. Use proactively after edits that add a branch to a category chain, a switch case or a table row.

entries.name: test-case-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer that maps existing tests to a routine's contract: normal, boundary, invalid and defensive cases, and tests tied to implementation. Use proactively after edits that add or change tests, validation, boundaries or table-driven logic.

entries.name: test-writer
entries.description: Implementer that writes tests from a routine's contract: normal, boundary, invalid and defensive cases. Edits test files only. Use when test-case findings or a test matrix call for tests, or before changing behavior.

entries.name: trust-boundary-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of inputs that cross a trust boundary: what is validated, rejected, recovered from, asserted and kept diagnosable. Use proactively after edits that add handlers, parsers, readers, consumers, endpoints, config keys or public functions.

entries.name: tuning-reviewer
entries.description: Reviewer of the evidence behind a performance change: requirement, baseline, single change, remeasurement and the stated clarity trade-off. Use proactively after edits described as optimization or speedup, or that add caching or manual loop tricks.

entries.name: audit
entries.description: Scan a directory or repository for data-contract health and return concerns rated healthy, watch or hot, with ranked hot spots, in at most 40 lines.
entries.argumentHint: [directory | glob | empty for the repository root]

entries.name: batch-jobs
entries.description: Use when writing or reviewing a batch job, ETL, nightly report, backfill, reprocessing run or MapReduce-style pipeline. Makes inputs and outputs recomputable and keeps side effects out of replayable work. Event-time streaming is stream-processing.

entries.name: checklist
entries.description: Walk the ten-item review checklist for the current change one item at a time, with evidence and a next action for each no.
entries.argumentHint: [paths | git ref | empty for the current diff]

entries.name: compat-matrix
entries.description: Build the old-and-new compatibility matrix for one schema, API, message or enum change and order the rollout so no reader meets a form it cannot read.
entries.argumentHint: [change description | migration or schema path | empty to use the contract files in the current diff]

entries.name: consistency-check
entries.description: Map every read path in a scope to its freshness need, where it is served from and the guarantee it gets, plus the conflict model for concurrent writes, in at most 40 lines.
entries.argumentHint: [feature | directory | entity name | empty for the repository root]

entries.name: consistency-contract
entries.description: Use when reads may be stale, a user must see their own write, caches or replicas serve reads, or two clients may edit one record. Makes freshness, visibility and conflict handling a contract. Races inside one transaction are transactions-and-isolation; replica mechanics are replication-topology.

entries.name: data-model-choice
entries.description: Use when picking or reviewing a data model or query style: relational, document, graph, key-value or analytical; schema shape; SQL versus application-side joins. Index and engine choice is storage-and-indexing.

entries.name: data-path-tests
entries.description: Use when writing or reviewing tests for consumers, jobs, handlers, projections, migrations or schema changes. Covers duplicate delivery, out-of-order messages, replay, conflict resolution, schema compatibility and rebuild or repair of derived views.

entries.name: derived-data
entries.description: Use when adding or changing a cache, search index, read model, projection, materialized view or denormalized field, or when one is stale, drifting or cannot be rebuilt. Defines propagation, lag visibility and rebuild. Who owns the truth is source-of-truth.

entries.name: encoding-and-evolution
entries.description: Use when changing a schema, column, API field, message, enum or status value, choosing JSON, Protocol Buffers, Avro or Thrift, or planning a rolling upgrade across old and new readers and writers. Event meaning and ids are event-design.

entries.name: event-design
entries.description: Use when defining or changing a command, event, log topic or materialized view contract, or the consumers of a durable log. Separates commands from facts and sets identifiers, metadata and versions. Payload compatibility is encoding-and-evolution; processors are stream-processing.

entries.name: explain-rule
entries.description: Explain one rule of the Designing Data-Intensive Applications rule set: its modal strength, the reason, how to check it, a small example and where the source allows an exception.
entries.argumentHint: [rule name | section name | phrase | empty to list the sections]

entries.name: faults-and-coordination
entries.description: Use when code relies on timeouts, wall-clock timestamps, locks, leases, leader election, majority votes, coordination services or consensus, or claims linearizability. Requires a fault model, monotonic clocks and fencing. Failover and replica data are replication-topology.

entries.name: fix
entries.description: Resolve named data-contract findings with the smallest change per finding, run the tests, never commit, and stop to ask before any contract or stored-data change.
entries.argumentHint: [findings text | path to a findings file | finding numbers from the last review]

entries.name: idempotent-handlers
entries.description: Use when code may run twice: command handlers, queue consumers, jobs, webhooks, retried calls, or any exactly-once claim. Applies deduplication keys and idempotent state transitions. Event order is ordering-scope; a caller's timeout is write-acknowledgment.

entries.name: invariant-map
entries.description: List the business invariants in a scope, the mechanism that enforces each, the isolation in effect and the anomaly still possible (lost update, write skew, phantom), in at most 40 lines.
entries.argumentHint: [module | feature | invariant in words | empty for the repository root]

entries.name: load-and-latency
entries.description: Use when someone claims a design will scale, proposes more nodes, caches or sharding for speed, or reports slowness. Demands load parameters, percentile latency and a named bottleneck first. Skewed keys are partitioning-locality.

entries.name: ordering-scope
entries.description: Use when events or updates for one entity can arrive out of order, parallel consumers touch the same key, code assumes global order, or last write wins by arrival. Scopes ordering per key or partition and adds versions. Duplicates are idempotent-handlers.

entries.name: ownership-map
entries.description: Inventory the datasets in a scope with their class, owner, writers, derived copies, propagation, lag visibility and rebuild path, in at most 40 lines.
entries.argumentHint: [directory | service name | dataset name | empty for the repository root]

entries.name: partitioning-locality
entries.description: Use when choosing a partition, shard or routing key, spreading data across nodes, handling hot keys or skew, or seeing queries and transactions that cross partitions. Colocates data and work by the key that drives consistency or aggregation.

entries.name: plan
entries.description: Plan a non-trivial change to a data path before editing: the five questions, touched concerns, rollout order, tests and observability.
entries.argumentHint: [change description | issue text | empty to plan from the current diff]

entries.name: principles
entries.description: Applies the Designing Data-Intensive Applications rule set to data-system work. Use for any task that changes how data is stored, copied, retried, ordered, versioned, replicated or processed, where ownership, consistency or failure behavior matter.

entries.name: replay-drill
entries.description: Walk one consumer, job or handler through duplicate, reordered, late, crash, restart and full-replay scenarios by reading the code, and report the predicted outcome of each.
entries.argumentHint: [consumer | job | handler path or name | empty for the one in the current diff]

entries.name: replication-topology
entries.description: Use when choosing or reviewing leader-follower, multi-leader or leaderless replication, sync versus async followers, failover, quorums, replica read routing or replica conflict resolution. Freshness promises are consistency-contract; locks and leases are faults-and-coordination.

entries.name: review
entries.description: Review a diff or paths against the Designing Data-Intensive Applications rules and report ranked findings by data concern.
entries.argumentHint: [paths | git ref | empty for the current diff]

entries.name: service-boundaries
entries.description: Use when splitting or merging services, designing an API between services or teams, or adding a cross-service call on a hot path. Aligns boundaries with data ownership. One dataset's owner is source-of-truth; wire formats are encoding-and-evolution.

entries.name: source-of-truth
entries.description: Use when the same data lives in several places, a cache or copy is written directly, two services update one fact, or ownership is unclear. Names the primary owner, derived copies, update path and repair. Rebuilding a copy is derived-data.

entries.name: storage-and-indexing
entries.description: Use when adding or reviewing an index, choosing between LSM-tree and B-tree engines, separating OLTP from analytics, or tuning write-heavy or scan-heavy tables. Covers secondary index cost, columnar layouts and memory residency. Model shape is data-model-choice.

entries.name: stream-processing
entries.description: Use when writing or reviewing a stream processor, windowed aggregate, stream join, change data capture or event sourcing. Sets event, processing and ingestion time, windows, lateness, state, checkpoints and guarantees. Batch is batch-jobs; one handler's retries are idempotent-handlers.

entries.name: transactions-and-isolation
entries.description: Use when a change must be atomic across rows or systems, an isolation level is chosen, a check-then-write may race (lost update, write skew, phantom), or a handler writes several stores or sends effects around a commit. Reader freshness: consistency-contract; caller's view: write-acknowledgment.

entries.name: write-acknowledgment
entries.description: Use when a write, command or request ends in success, timeout or error and you must say what happened: accepted, persisted, applied or durable, including unknown outcomes. Run-twice receivers are idempotent-handlers; atomicity is transactions-and-isolation.

entries.name: write-path-trace
entries.description: Follow one write step by step and record what is durable and visible after each step, what a crash or timeout there leaves behind, how a retry behaves and how the state is repaired.
